learn.hook: That marigold garland at a Diwali doorway is not just decoration: every flower in it is a complete reproductive factory, built long before it opened.
points: Flowers are the sites of sexual reproduction in angiosperms. They also carry aesthetic, ornamental, social and cultural value in festivals, worship and gifting.
Pre-fertilisation events start well before a flower opens: hormonal and structural changes turn a shoot apex into a floral primordium, which develops into the flower bud.
The androecium (whorl of stamens) is the male reproductive organ; the gynoecium (pistil) is the female reproductive organ.

A stamen has a long slender stalk, the filament, and a terminal anther. A typical angiosperm anther is bilobed, and each lobe has two theca, so the anther is dithecous. In transverse section it is tetragonal with four microsporangia, one at each corner; these develop into pollen sacs.

The microsporangium wall has four layers from outside in: epidermis, endothecium, middle layers and tapetum. The outer three protect and help dehiscence; the innermost tapetum nourishes developing pollen, and its cells have dense cytoplasm and usually more than one nucleus.

example.q: A student sees a transverse section of a young anther with four groups of cells, one at each corner, each ringed by four layers. Identify the structures and the role of the innermost layer.
steps: Four corner groups = four microsporangia, so the anther is bilobed and dithecous (2 lobes × 2 theca).
The four wall layers outside to inside are epidermis, endothecium, middle layers and tapetum.
The tapetum lines the sporogenous tissue and nourishes the developing pollen grains.
example.answer: Four microsporangia (pollen sacs); innermost tapetum nourishes the developing pollen.

learn.reallife: From Bengal's lotus in Durga Puja to jasmine gajras in Chennai, Indian life is packed with flowers. A floriculture start-up selling cut roses is really selling reproductive organs that the plant built to make seeds.

quiz.q: How many microsporangia are present in a typical dithecous angiosperm anther?
quiz.explain: A bilobed anther has two theca per lobe, and each theca has one microsporangium, giving four in all, one at each corner of the tetragonal section.
steps: Asked: number of microsporangia in a dithecous anther
Typical anther is bilobed; each lobe has 2 theca, each theca one microsporangium
2 lobes × 2 theca = 4 microsporangia, one at each corner
Answer: 4
quiz.mistake: Counts only the two lobes and forgets that each lobe has two theca

quiz.q: Which layer of the microsporangium wall nourishes the developing pollen grains?
quiz.explain: The tapetum is the innermost wall layer; its cells, with dense cytoplasm and often more than one nucleus, nourish the developing pollen.
steps: Asked: which wall layer feeds the developing pollen
Wall layers outside → in: epidermis, endothecium, middle layers, tapetum
Only the innermost tapetum nourishes the pollen; outer three protect and help dehiscence
Answer: Tapetum
quiz.mistake: Thinks the fibrous endothecium feeds the pollen because it is a large layer

quiz.q: Tapetal cells are characterised by
options: dense cytoplasm and generally more than one nucleus
thick lignified walls and a single nucleus
quiz.explain: Tapetal cells are metabolically very active nourishing cells, so they have dense cytoplasm and are often multinucleate.
steps: Asked: the features of tapetal cells
Tapetum is a nourishing, metabolically active layer
Its cells have dense cytoplasm and generally more than one nucleus
Answer: dense cytoplasm and generally more than one nucleus
quiz.mistake: Confuses the nourishing tapetum with protective, thick-walled outer layers

quiz.q: Which statement about pre-fertilisation events is correct?
options: They begin only after the pollen lands on the stigma
They consist only of the opening of the flower bud
They take place only inside the ovary after fertilisation
Hormonal and structural changes lead to the differentiation of a floral primordium well before the flower is seen
quiz.explain: Pre-fertilisation events begin long before a flower appears: hormonal and structural changes initiate differentiation of the floral primordium.
steps: Asked: when pre-fertilisation events begin
They start well before the flower is seen, while the shoot apex is changing
Hormonal and structural changes turn the shoot apex into a floral primordium → flower bud
So the correct statement is the one about the floral primordium differentiating early
Answer: Hormonal and structural changes lead to the differentiation of a floral primordium well before the flower is seen

quiz.q: The outer three wall layers of a microsporangium (epidermis, endothecium, middle layers) mainly
options: form the pollen grains by meiosis
protect the sporangium and help in dehiscence of the anther to release pollen
quiz.explain: The outer three layers perform protection and help in dehiscence; nourishment is the job of the tapetum, and pollen arises from sporogenous tissue.
steps: Asked: role of epidermis, endothecium and middle layers
These outer three layers protect the microsporangium and help the anther dehisce
Nourishing is the tapetum's job; pollen comes from sporogenous tissue
Answer: protect the sporangium and help in dehiscence of the anther to release pollen
quiz.mistake: Assigns the tapetum's nourishing role to all four wall layers

quiz.q: Assertion (A): The male reproductive organ of a flower is the androecium. Reason (R): The androecium is a whorl of stamens.
options: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
quiz.explain: The androecium, a whorl of stamens that produce pollen, represents the male reproductive organ; R defines it and so explains A.
steps: A: androecium is the male reproductive organ – true
R: androecium is a whorl of stamens, which produce pollen – true
Being a whorl of pollen-making stamens is why it is the male organ, so R explains A
Answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A

quiz.q: In a T.S. of a mature anther, the tetragonal outline is because
options: four pollen grains are formed in each anther
the four microsporangia lie one at each corner
quiz.explain: The anther is bilobed, but its four microsporangia sit at the four corners, giving a four-cornered (tetragonal) section.
steps: Asked: why the anther T.S. looks four-cornered
The anther has 2 lobes but 4 microsporangia
The 4 microsporangia sit one at each corner, giving a tetragonal outline
Answer: the four microsporangia lie one at each corner
quiz.mistake: Thinks the anther has four lobes rather than two lobes with two theca each

quiz.q: Which of these is an example of the social and cultural value of flowers rather than their reproductive role?
options: Exchanging flower garlands at a wedding
Forming an embryo sac in the ovule
quiz.explain: Garland exchange is a cultural use of flowers; the other options are reproductive functions.
steps: Asked: a cultural use of flowers, not a reproductive one
Pollen, embryo sac and seeds are all parts of reproduction
Garland exchange at a wedding is a social and cultural use
Answer: Exchanging flower garlands at a wedding
quiz.mistake: Does not separate the biological function of a flower from its human uses

teach.praise: Chirp! Stamens are male, the pistil is female, and the anther's four pollen sacs are fed by the tapetum. Lovely!
teach.nudge: Nice! Now tell me what the anther holds inside, and which wall layer feeds the pollen.

revise.summary: Flowers are the sites of sexual reproduction in angiosperms. The stamen has a filament and a bilobed, dithecous anther with four microsporangia whose four-layered wall ends in the nourishing tapetum.

learn.hook: Pollen grains survive as fossils for millions of years and can still be identified under a microscope. Their secret armour, sporopollenin, laughs at strong acids.
points: Sporogenous tissue fills the centre of a young microsporangium. Each cell is a potential pollen (microspore) mother cell, PMC, and is diploid.

Microsporogenesis: each microspore mother cell divides by meiosis to form a cluster of four haploid cells, the microspore tetrad. As the anther matures and dehydrates, the microspores separate and develop into pollen grains.

The pollen wall has two layers. The hard outer exine is made of sporopollenin, one of the most resistant organic materials known; it withstands high temperature, strong acids and alkalis, and no enzyme is known to degrade it. Germ pores are apertures where sporopollenin is absent. The thin inner intine is made of cellulose and pectin.
A mature pollen grain has two cells: a large vegetative cell with abundant food reserve and a large irregular nucleus, and a small spindle-shaped generative cell floating in its cytoplasm.
In over 60 per cent of angiosperms pollen is shed at this 2-celled stage. In the rest, the generative cell divides mitotically to give two male gametes before shedding (3-celled stage).

example.q: One microspore mother cell undergoes meiosis. How many pollen grains form and what is their ploidy? If the pollen is shed at the 3-celled stage, how many male gametes does each grain carry?
steps: Meiosis of one diploid PMC gives a tetrad of four haploid microspores.
Each microspore matures into one pollen grain, so 4 pollen grains, each haploid (n).
In the 3-celled stage, the generative cell has already divided by mitosis into two male gametes.
example.answer: 4 haploid pollen grains; 2 male gametes in each 3-celled grain.

learn.reallife: Archaeologists in India use fossil pollen in lake sediments to reconstruct ancient monsoon patterns and crops of the Harappan period, all thanks to sporopollenin.

quiz.q: How many pollen grains are produced from 25 microspore mother cells?
quiz.explain: Each microspore mother cell gives a tetrad of four microspores by meiosis, and each microspore becomes one pollen grain.
steps: Given: 25 microspore mother cells (PMCs)
Each PMC divides by meiosis → tetrad of 4 microspores; each microspore → 1 pollen grain
Pollen grains = 25 × 4 = 100
Answer: 100
quiz.mistake: Thinks one mother cell makes one pollen grain

quiz.q: The exine of the pollen grain is made of
quiz.explain: Exine is made of sporopollenin, an extremely resistant organic material; cellulose and pectin make the intine.
steps: Asked: material of the exine
Exine (outer wall) = sporopollenin; intine (inner wall) = cellulose and pectin
Answer: sporopollenin
quiz.mistake: Swaps the materials of exine and intine

quiz.q: Pollen grains are well preserved as fossils because
options: the intine is made of lignin
the generative cell stays alive for millions of years
pollen grains are always buried in water
sporopollenin in the exine resists high temperature, strong acids and alkalis and enzyme attack
quiz.explain: Sporopollenin is among the most resistant organic materials and no enzyme is known to degrade it, so the exine survives for ages.
steps: Asked: why pollen survives as fossils
The exine is made of sporopollenin, one of the most resistant organic materials
It withstands high temperature, strong acids and alkalis, and no enzyme degrades it
Answer: sporopollenin in the exine resists high temperature, strong acids and alkalis and enzyme attack
quiz.mistake: Credits the intine instead of the exine

quiz.q: In what percentage of angiosperms are pollen grains shed at the 2-celled stage, according to NCERT?
quiz.explain: Pollen in over 60 per cent of angiosperms is shed at the 2-celled stage (vegetative + generative cell); the rest at the 3-celled stage.
steps: Asked: share of angiosperms shedding pollen at the 2-celled stage
NCERT: over 60 per cent shed pollen with a vegetative and a generative cell
The rest shed at the 3-celled stage
Answer: Over 60 per cent
quiz.mistake: Assumes all pollen is shed with two male gametes ready

quiz.q: Germ pores on a pollen grain are
options: pores in the intine through which nutrients leave
regions of the exine where sporopollenin is absent
quiz.explain: Germ pores are apertures in the exine lacking sporopollenin; the pollen tube emerges through one of them.
steps: Asked: what germ pores are
Germ pores are apertures in the exine where sporopollenin is absent
The pollen tube comes out through a germ pore
Answer: regions of the exine where sporopollenin is absent
quiz.mistake: Thinks germ pores belong to the anther wall

quiz.q: Which statement about the two cells of a mature pollen grain is correct?
options: The vegetative cell is larger with abundant food reserve; the generative cell is small and spindle-shaped
The generative cell is larger and stores food
Both cells are the same size and identical
The vegetative cell divides to form the male gametes
quiz.explain: The generative cell (not the vegetative cell) divides mitotically to give two male gametes; the vegetative cell is the big food-rich cell.
steps: Asked: correct description of the two pollen cells
Vegetative cell: large, abundant food reserve, large irregular nucleus
Generative cell: small, spindle-shaped, floats in the vegetative cell's cytoplasm
It is the generative cell, not the vegetative cell, that forms male gametes
Answer: The vegetative cell is larger with abundant food reserve; the generative cell is small and spindle-shaped
quiz.mistake: Mixes up which cell forms the male gametes

quiz.q: The division that converts a microspore mother cell into a microspore tetrad is
quiz.explain: Microspore mother cells are diploid and form haploid microspores, so the division must be meiosis.
steps: Asked: division that turns a PMC into a tetrad
PMC is diploid (2n); microspores are haploid (n)
Only meiosis halves the chromosome number and gives 4 cells
Answer: meiosis
quiz.mistake: Forgets that pollen is haploid while the mother cell is diploid

quiz.q: The male gametes in a 3-celled pollen grain arise from
options: meiotic division of the vegetative cell
meiotic division of the generative cell
mitotic division of the generative cell
quiz.explain: The haploid generative cell divides by mitosis to form two haploid male gametes; no meiosis happens inside the pollen grain.
steps: Asked: origin of the male gametes in 3-celled pollen
The generative cell is already haploid
It divides by mitosis into two haploid male gametes; no meiosis happens in pollen
Answer: mitotic division of the generative cell
quiz.mistake: Thinks a second meiosis occurs inside the pollen

revise.summary: Each diploid microspore mother cell divides by meiosis into a tetrad of four haploid microspores that become pollen grains. Pollen has a sporopollenin exine and a cellulose-pectin intine and holds a vegetative and a generative cell.

topics.title: Pollen viability, allergy and pollen banks

learn.hook: If your nose runs every time a weed called carrot grass flowers in your city, you have met pollen biology the hard way.
points: Pollen of many species causes allergies and bronchial afflictions (chronic respiratory disorders such as asthma and bronchitis). Parthenium (carrot grass), which entered India as a contaminant with imported wheat, is ubiquitous and a major cause of pollen allergy.
Pollen grains are rich in nutrients. Pollen tablets and syrups are used as food supplements and are claimed to improve the performance of athletes and race horses.

Viability is the period for which pollen can still fertilise. It depends on temperature and humidity. In rice and wheat pollen loses viability within about 30 minutes of release; in some members of Rosaceae, Leguminosae and Solanaceae it stays viable for months.
Pollen of many species can be stored for years in liquid nitrogen at −196 °C (cryopreservation). Such stores, called pollen banks, work like seed banks and are used in crop breeding programmes.

example.q: A rice breeder collects pollen at 10:00 a.m. and plans to dust it on emasculated flowers at 11:30 a.m. the same day without storage. Will it work? Suggest a fix.
steps: Rice pollen loses viability within about 30 minutes of release.
90 minutes is three times that limit, so the pollen will most likely be non-viable.
Either use fresh pollen within minutes or cryopreserve it in liquid nitrogen at −196 °C.
example.answer: No; rice pollen dies within ~30 min. Use fresh pollen or store it in liquid nitrogen (−196 °C).

learn.reallife: ICAR institutes keep cryo-stored germplasm so breeders in Cuttack or Ludhiana can cross varieties that flower at different times or places.

Those conditions are temperature and humidity

learn.hook: An ovule is a plant's safe vault: layers of armour, one tiny door called the micropyle, and a single precious cell that will become the egg's home.
points: The gynoecium may have a single pistil (monocarpellary) or more than one (multicarpellary). When there is more than one, the pistils may be fused (syncarpous, e.g. Papaver) or free (apocarpous, e.g. Michelia). Each pistil has stigma, style and ovary.

Inside the ovary is the ovarian cavity (locule); the placenta inside bears the megasporangia, commonly called ovules. The number of ovules may be one (wheat, paddy, mango) to many (papaya, watermelon, orchids).

Ovule structure: it is attached to the placenta by a stalk, the funicle; the junction of ovule body and funicle is the hilum. Protective envelopes called integuments surround the ovule except at a small opening, the micropyle. Opposite the micropyle is the chalaza, the basal part. Inside the integuments is the nucellus, a mass of cells with food reserve, which holds the embryo sac (female gametophyte).

Megasporogenesis: a single megaspore mother cell (MMC), large with dense cytoplasm, differentiates in the micropylar region of the nucellus. It divides by meiosis to give four haploid megaspores. In most flowering plants one megaspore is functional and the other three degenerate.

example.q: An ovule has 2n = 24 chromosomes in its nucellus cells. How many chromosomes will the megaspore mother cell, each megaspore and the functional megaspore have?
steps: The MMC is a nucellar (sporophytic) cell, so it is diploid: 24.
Meiosis halves the number, so each of the four megaspores has 12.
The functional megaspore is one of these, so it also has 12.
example.answer: MMC 24; each megaspore 12; functional megaspore 12.

learn.reallife: A papaya you slice for breakfast hides hundreds of ovules-turned-seeds, while a mango hides just one: ovule number per ovary decides how many seeds you spit out.

quiz.q: How many functional megaspores are typically formed from one megaspore mother cell in most flowering plants?

quiz.q: Papaver has a multicarpellary gynoecium with fused pistils. This condition is called

Fused pistils = syncarpous (Papaver); free pistils = apocarpous (Michelia)
Answer: syncarpous

quiz.q: The stalk by which an ovule is attached to the placenta is the

That stalk is the funicle
The hilum is only the junction of ovule body and funicle
Answer: funicle

quiz.q: The megaspore mother cell differentiates in which region of the nucellus?
quiz.explain: Ovules generally have a single MMC in the micropylar region of the nucellus.

A single MMC differentiates in the micropylar region of the nucellus
Answer: Micropylar region

quiz.q: The nucellus is best described as
options: a mass of cells with reserve food enclosed by the integuments, holding the embryo sac
the outer protective layer of the ovule
the opening through which the pollen tube enters
quiz.explain: Nucellus cells have abundant food and the embryo sac lies within the nucellus.

Nucellus = mass of cells with food reserve, inside the integuments

quiz.q: If the nucellus of an ovule has 2n = 16, the chromosome number in a functional megaspore will be

steps: Nucellus/MMC: 2n = 16
Meiosis halves: n = 16/2 = 8
Answer: 8

quiz.q: The opening at the tip of the ovule, left uncovered by the integuments, is the
quiz.explain: Integuments enclose the ovule except at the micropyle, the usual entry point of the pollen tube.
steps: Asked: the opening at the tip of the ovule
Integuments cover the ovule except at a small opening
That opening is the micropyle; the chalaza is the opposite, basal end
Answer: micropyle
quiz.mistake: Mixes up micropyle and chalaza, which lie at opposite ends

topics.title: The embryo sac and ploidy of cells

learn.hook: Seven cells, eight nuclei, one tiny sac: the angiosperm embryo sac is the most efficient studio apartment in biology.
points: The functional megaspore develops into the female gametophyte (embryo sac). This method, from a single megaspore, is monosporic development.

The nucleus of the functional megaspore divides mitotically into two nuclei that move to opposite poles (2-nucleate). Two more sequential mitotic divisions give 4-nucleate and then 8-nucleate stages. These are free-nuclear divisions; cell walls form only after the 8-nucleate stage.

Organisation: three cells at the micropylar end form the egg apparatus (two synergids + one egg cell). Synergids carry special thickenings at the micropylar tip, the filiform apparatus, which guides pollen tubes into the synergid. Three cells at the chalazal end are antipodals. The large central cell holds two polar nuclei. So a typical embryo sac is 8-nucleate and 7-celled.

Ploidy check: nucellus, integuments, MMC, PMC and tapetum are 2n; microspores, pollen cells, megaspores, egg, synergids, antipodals and polar nuclei are n; the zygote is 2n and the primary endosperm nucleus is 3n.

example.q: Why is a typical angiosperm embryo sac described as 8-nucleate but 7-celled?
steps: Three mitotic divisions of the functional megaspore nucleus give 2³ = 8 nuclei.
Six of these form six cells: 3 at micropylar end (2 synergids + egg) and 3 antipodals at chalazal end.
The remaining two polar nuclei share one large central cell.
example.answer: 8 nuclei, but 6 single-nucleus cells + 1 central cell with 2 polar nuclei = 7 cells.

learn.reallife: An IVF lab in Mumbai checks human embryos at 8 cells, but plant breeders at IARI count 8 nuclei in a 7-celled embryo sac. Same number, very different biology.

learn.hook: A flower that never opens yet sets seed every time sounds like a magic trick. Viola, Oxalis and Commelina pull it off routinely.
points: Pollination is the transfer of pollen grains from the anther to the stigma of a pistil.

Autogamy: pollen transferred to the stigma of the same flower. Geitonogamy: transfer to another flower of the same plant; functionally cross-pollination with an agent, but genetically similar to autogamy. Xenogamy: transfer to the stigma of a different plant; the only type that brings genetically different pollen.

Chasmogamous flowers have exposed anthers and stigma, like normal flowers. Cleistogamous flowers never open, so anthers and stigma lie close together; when anthers dehisce, pollen contacts the stigma directly.

Cleistogamous flowers are invariably autogamous, so they produce assured seed set even without pollinators. Viola (common pansy), Oxalis and Commelina bear both chasmogamous and cleistogamous flowers.

example.q: A pumpkin vine has male and female flowers. Bees move pollen from a male flower to a female flower on the same vine. Name this pollination and its genetic consequence.
steps: Pollen goes to a different flower, so it is not autogamy.
The flowers are on the same plant, so it is not xenogamy.
This is geitonogamy: it needs an agent like cross-pollination, but the pollen is genetically the same as the plant's own.
example.answer: Geitonogamy; genetically equivalent to autogamy.

learn.reallife: In Maharashtra's onion seed fields, growers rent bee boxes to ensure xenogamy, because cross-pollinated onion gives far better seed than selfed plants.

learn.hook: That golden dust drifting off a maize field in Bihar is a plant betting its future on the breeze.
points: Agents of pollination are abiotic (wind, water) and biotic (animals). Most plants use biotic agents; among abiotic agents, wind is far more common than water.

Wind-pollinated flowers: light, non-sticky pollen; well-exposed stamens; large, often feathery stigma to trap pollen; usually a single ovule in each ovary; numerous flowers packed in an inflorescence. Common in grasses. The silky threads of a corn cob (called 'tassels' in NCERT) are the stigma and style waving in the wind. (Botanically these threads are the corn 'silk'; the tassel at the top of the maize plant is the male flower cluster.)

Water pollination is quite rare, limited to about 30 genera, mostly monocots: Vallisneria and Hydrilla (fresh water) and Zostera (marine sea-grasses). Pollen is protected from wetting by a mucilaginous covering.

In Vallisneria, female flowers reach the water surface on long stalks and male flowers or pollen are released onto the surface and carried passively by currents. In sea-grasses, female flowers stay submerged and long ribbon-like pollen is released inside the water.
Not all aquatic plants use water: in water hyacinth and water lily the flowers emerge above the water and are pollinated by insects or wind.

example.q: A flower has a large feathery stigma, dull petals, no nectar and light, dry pollen. Predict its agent and give two more features you would expect.
steps: Feathery stigma and light non-sticky pollen suit trapping airborne pollen.
No nectar or colour means no animal is being attracted.
Agent: wind. Expect well-exposed stamens, a single ovule per ovary and many flowers in an inflorescence.
example.answer: Wind pollination; also exposed stamens, single ovule per ovary, crowded inflorescence.

learn.reallife: Sugarcane, wheat and rice that feed India are all grasses; their wind-pollinated flowers explain why farmers never need beehives in a paddy field.

learn.hook: One Amorphophallus flower towers about 6 feet tall and smells like rotting meat, all to lure a few insects.
points: Most flowering plants use animals. Bees are the dominant biotic pollinators; others include butterflies, flies, beetles, wasps, ants, moths, birds (sunbirds and hummingbirds) and bats. Some primates (lemurs), arboreal rodents and reptiles (gecko and garden lizard) have also been reported.

Insect-pollinated flowers are generally large, colourful, fragrant and rich in nectar. Small flowers group into inflorescences to be conspicuous. Flowers pollinated by flies and beetles often secrete foul odours. Pollen is generally sticky.
Floral rewards keep visitors coming: nectar and pollen grains. When the animal touches anther and stigma, its body gets coated with pollen, which it carries to the stigma of another flower.

Some flowers give safe places to lay eggs. Amorphophallus (about 6 feet tall) does this. In Yucca, a moth species and the plant cannot complete their life cycles without each other: the moth lays eggs in the ovary locule, the flower is pollinated, and the larvae feed on developing seeds.
Pollen or nectar robbers consume the rewards without bringing about pollination.

topics.title: Outbreeding, pollen-pistil interaction and artificial hybridisation

learn.hook: Plants cannot pick partners, yet they have clever ways of refusing their own pollen. Breeders at IARI exploit these rules daily.
points: Continued self-pollination causes inbreeding depression, so plants evolved outbreeding devices: (1) pollen release and stigma receptivity not synchronised; (2) anther and stigma at different positions; (3) self-incompatibility, a genetic mechanism that stops self-pollen from germinating or growing a tube; (4) unisexual flowers.

Castor and maize are monoecious (male and female flowers on the same plant): this prevents autogamy but not geitonogamy. Papaya is dioecious (male and female flowers on different plants): this prevents both autogamy and geitonogamy.

Pollen-pistil interaction: the pistil recognises compatible pollen of the right type through chemical components. Compatible pollen germinates and a pollen tube grows through the stigma and style to the ovary, enters the ovule through the micropyle, and enters a synergid through the filiform apparatus. Incompatible pollen is rejected.

Artificial hybridisation: emasculation removes anthers from a bisexual flower bud before dehiscence; bagging covers it with butter paper to prevent contamination; when the stigma is receptive, desired pollen is dusted on and the flower is rebagged. Female flowers of unisexual plants need no emasculation, only bagging.

example.q: Exam-style: Differentiate geitonogamy and xenogamy, and name a plant whose flower type prevents both autogamy and geitonogamy.
steps: Geitonogamy: pollen to another flower of the same plant; genetically like selfing.
Xenogamy: pollen to a flower of a different plant; brings genetic variation.
Dioecious plants such as papaya carry male and female flowers on different plants, ruling out both selfing types.
example.answer: Geitonogamy = same plant; xenogamy = different plant. Papaya (dioecious) prevents both autogamy and geitonogamy.

learn.reallife: Hybrid cotton seed in Gujarat is still produced by hand emasculation and pollination; teams of workers bag thousands of flowers every season.

options: a genetic mechanism that prevents self-pollen from fertilising ovules by blocking germination or tube growth
the inability of a flower to produce pollen
the death of the ovule after pollination

It is a genetic mechanism
It stops self-pollen from germinating or growing a tube on the pistil
Answer: a genetic mechanism that prevents self-pollen from fertilising ovules by blocking germination or tube growth

covering the flower with a bag

Emasculation = removing anthers from a bisexual bud before they dehisce
Bagging and dusting pollen are separate later steps

To prevent contamination of its stigma with unwanted pollen

the integuments and then the egg directly
the funicle and then the central cell
the micropyle and then a synergid via the filiform apparatus

steps: Path of the pollen tube: stigma → style → ovary
It enters the ovule through the micropyle
The filiform apparatus guides it into a synergid
Answer: the micropyle and then a synergid via the filiform apparatus

quiz.q: In a unisexual plant, a breeder wants to cross-pollinate the female flowers. Which step is NOT needed?

quiz.explain: Female flowers have no anthers, so there is nothing to emasculate; bagging is still needed.
steps: A female flower of a unisexual plant has no anthers
Emasculation means removing anthers, so it is not needed
Bagging, dusting and rebagging are still needed
Answer: Emasculation

quiz.q: Assertion (A): The pistil can accept compatible pollen and reject incompatible pollen. Reason (R): The pistil recognises pollen through chemical components produced by pollen interacting with those of the pistil.
options: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
A is false, but R is true

teach.ask: Gappu wants to make a super tomato: 'How do plants avoid selfing, and how would I make a hybrid myself?'

revise.summary: Plants avoid inbreeding depression with outbreeding devices such as unsynchronised maturity, separate positions, self-incompatibility and unisexual flowers. The pistil chemically recognises compatible pollen, and breeders use emasculation and bagging for artificial hybridisation.
focus: Outbreeding devices; monoecious vs dioecious plants
Path of the pollen tube into the embryo sac
remember: Monoecious (castor, maize): stops autogamy, not geitonogamy
Dioecious (papaya): stops both autogamy and geitonogamy
Emasculation = remove anthers before dehiscence; bagging = butter paper cover
Pollen tube: micropyle → synergid via filiform apparatus
traps: Don't emasculate female flowers of unisexual plants; only bag them
Don't confuse emasculation with bagging

learn.hook: Tender coconut water at a Chennai beach is literally liquid endosperm, made of thousands of free nuclei floating together.
points: After entering a synergid, the pollen tube releases two male gametes into its cytoplasm. Syngamy: one male gamete fuses with the egg cell to form a diploid zygote.
Triple fusion: the other male gamete fuses with the two polar nuclei in the central cell to form a triploid primary endosperm nucleus (PEN). The central cell becomes the primary endosperm cell (PEC).
Syngamy + triple fusion together = double fertilisation, an event unique to flowering plants. The PEC develops into endosperm; the zygote develops into the embryo.

Endosperm develops before the embryo. The PEC divides repeatedly to form triploid endosperm tissue full of reserve food. Commonly the PEN first undergoes free-nuclear divisions; cell walls form later and the endosperm becomes cellular. Tender coconut water is free-nuclear endosperm; the surrounding white kernel is cellular endosperm.
Endosperm may be fully consumed by the developing embryo before seed maturation (pea, groundnut, beans) or may persist in the mature seed (castor, coconut, cereals).

example.q: In a plant with 2n = 14, find the chromosome numbers in the zygote and the primary endosperm nucleus.
steps: n = 7. Egg (n) + male gamete (n) = zygote 2n = 14.
Two polar nuclei (n + n) + male gamete (n) = PEN 3n.
example.answer: Zygote 14; PEN 21.

learn.reallife: The atta in your roti comes mostly from the persistent endosperm of wheat grains, the same triple-fusion product described here.

learn.hook: When you sprout moong for a salad, the tiny root and shoot that pop out were already packed inside the seed as an embryo.
points: The embryo develops at the micropylar end of the embryo sac, where the zygote is. Most zygotes divide only after some endosperm has formed.
Stages: the zygote forms the proembryo, then the globular, heart-shaped and finally the mature embryo.

Dicot embryo: an embryonal axis with two cotyledons. The part above the cotyledons is the epicotyl, ending in the plumule (shoot tip); the part below is the hypocotyl, ending in the radicle (root tip), covered by the root cap.

Monocot embryo (e.g. grass family): one cotyledon, the scutellum, at one side of the axis. At the lower end, the radicle and root cap are enclosed in a sheath, the coleorhiza. The epicotyl has the shoot apex and a few leaf primordia enclosed in a hollow foliar structure, the coleoptile.

Diagram skill: in labelling, show the anther T.S. (four microsporangia, wall layers), pollen (exine, intine, germ pore, two cells), anatropous ovule (funicle, hilum, integuments, micropyle, chalaza, nucellus, embryo sac), embryo sac (egg apparatus, antipodals, polar nuclei) and both embryos.

example.q: A seedling's root emerges through a protective sheath and the shoot through a hollow leaf-like sheath. Is it a monocot or dicot? Name both sheaths.
steps: Sheaths over root and shoot are characteristic of grass-family monocots.
The root sheath is the coleorhiza; the shoot sheath is the coleoptile.
example.answer: Monocot; root sheath = coleorhiza, shoot sheath = coleoptile.

learn.reallife: Germinating maize in a Karnataka seed lab shows a coleoptile poking up like a sheath, while sprouted chana shows two fleshy cotyledons: a ready-made comparison for your practical file.

games.title: Dicot or monocot embryo?

quiz.q: The single cotyledon of a monocot (grass) embryo is called the

In the grass family the single cotyledon is the scutellum, at one side of the axis

learn.hook: A 2000-year-old date palm seed from near the Dead Sea once sprouted. Seeds are nature's time capsules.
points: In angiosperms the seed is the final product of sexual reproduction: a fertilised ovule with seed coat(s), cotyledon(s) and an embryo axis. Non-albuminous (exalbuminous) seeds have no residual endosperm (pea, groundnut); albuminous seeds retain it (wheat, maize, barley, castor). In some seeds like black pepper and beet, remnants of nucellus persist: this residual nucellus is the perisperm.

Integuments harden into seed coats. The micropyle remains as a small pore that lets oxygen and water in during germination. As seeds mature, water content falls to 10–15 per cent moisture by mass; metabolic activity slows and the embryo may enter dormancy until conditions are favourable.

The ovary develops into the fruit and the ovules into seeds. The ovary wall becomes the pericarp. In most plants only the ovary forms the fruit (true fruits). In apple, strawberry and cashew the thalamus also contributes; these are false fruits.
Parthenocarpic fruits, such as banana, develop without fertilisation and are seedless. Parthenocarpy can be induced by applying growth hormones.

Advantages of seeds: pollination and fertilisation are independent of water; dispersal adaptations help colonise new areas; food reserves nourish seedlings; dormancy, hard seed coats protect; sexual reproduction creates variation. Viability can be enormous: a lupine (Lupinus arcticus) seed from the Arctic tundra germinated after about 10,000 years, and a date palm (Phoenix dactylifera) seed about 2000 years old was viable.

example.q: Classify: (a) castor seed, (b) groundnut seed, (c) apple, (d) banana, as albuminous/non-albuminous seed or true/false/parthenocarpic fruit.
steps: Castor keeps endosperm: albuminous seed.
Groundnut endosperm is consumed: non-albuminous seed.
Apple has thalamus contributing to the fruit: false fruit.
Banana develops without fertilisation: parthenocarpic fruit.
example.answer: (a) albuminous (b) non-albuminous (c) false fruit (d) parthenocarpic fruit

learn.reallife: India's national seed banks store crop seeds at very low moisture and temperature, building on the natural dormancy of dry seeds; it is why a farmer's seed can survive from one kharif season to the next.

quiz.q: A seed about 10,000 years old that germinated was of

Date palm (Phoenix dactylifera) seed was about 2000 years old
Answer: lupine (Lupinus arcticus)
quiz.mistake: Swaps the lupine and date palm records

Answer: perisperm

forms by apomixis with viable seeds

quiz.q: Which seed is albuminous?
quiz.explain: Castor retains endosperm in the mature seed; pea, groundnut and beans have it consumed.

Castor keeps it; pea, groundnut and bean use it up
Answer: Castor

Seeds can stay dormant through unfavourable periods

revise.summary: The seed is a fertilised ovule with seed coats, cotyledons and embryo axis; the ovary becomes the fruit. Seeds may be albuminous or non-albuminous, fruits may be true, false or parthenocarpic, and some seeds stay viable for thousands of years.

learn.hook: Farmers buy fresh hybrid seed every year because hybrid vigour fades. Apomixis could let them save seed and keep the vigour forever.
points: Apomixis is the formation of seeds without fertilisation. It is a form of asexual reproduction that mimics sexual reproduction. It is found in some species of Asteraceae and grasses.

Ways it can happen: (1) a diploid egg cell forms without reduction division and develops into an embryo without fertilisation; (2) in many species such as citrus and mango, some nucellar cells around the embryo sac start dividing, protrude into the embryo sac and develop into embryos.
Polyembryony is the occurrence of more than one embryo in a seed, as in an orange seed, where extra embryos arise from nucellar cells.

Hybrid seed is costly and must be bought every year because the progeny of hybrids segregate and lose hybrid characters. If hybrids are made into apomicts, there is no segregation, so farmers could keep using the same seed year after year.

example.q: Seeds of a citrus variety produced three seedlings each. Two were identical to the mother plant and one was different. Explain.
steps: Citrus shows polyembryony through nucellar embryos.
Nucellar cells are maternal diploid tissue, so their embryos are genetically identical to the mother (clones).
The odd one likely came from the zygote formed by fertilisation, so it carries genes from both parents.
example.answer: Two nucellar (apomictic) embryos = clones of the mother; one zygotic embryo = genetically different.

learn.reallife: Hybrid paddy and maize seed is a big business in India. Researchers are working on apomixis in rice so smallholders in Odisha could save and replant hybrid seed.

games.title: Asexual seeds?
items: It is asexual seed formation mimicking sexual reproduction.

learn.hook: Why do the testes sit outside the abdomen in the scrotum? Because sperm production needs a body part that is literally a little cooler than you.
points: Humans reproduce sexually and are viviparous (give birth to young ones). Reproductive events: gametogenesis (formation of gametes), insemination (transfer of sperms into the female genital tract), fertilisation (fusion of male and female gametes forming the zygote), cleavage and implantation (formation and attachment of the blastocyst to the uterine wall), gestation (embryonic development) and parturition (delivery of the baby).

These events begin after puberty. There are marked differences between males and females: in men sperm formation continues even in old age, whereas in women formation of ova ceases around the age of fifty years.

The male reproductive system lies in the pelvis. A pair of testes sits outside the abdominal cavity within a pouch called the scrotum, which keeps testicular temperature 2–2.5 °C lower than normal internal body temperature, necessary for spermatogenesis. In adults each testis is oval, about 4–5 cm long and 2–3 cm wide.
Each testis has about 250 compartments called testicular lobules. Each lobule contains one to three highly coiled seminiferous tubules, where sperms are produced.

Each seminiferous tubule is lined on its inside by male germ cells (spermatogonia) and Sertoli cells. Spermatogonia undergo meiotic divisions to form sperms; Sertoli cells provide nutrition to the germ cells. In the interstitial spaces outside the tubules lie small blood vessels and interstitial (Leydig) cells, which synthesise and secrete androgens, along with other immunologically competent cells.

steps: Minimum: 250 lobules × 1 tubule = 250.

example.answer: Between about 250 and 750 seminiferous tubules.

learn.hook: Sperms travel through a pipeline longer than you might expect, collecting fluids at each stop like a train collecting passengers at stations.
points: Male accessory ducts: rete testis, vasa efferentia, epididymis and vas deferens. Seminiferous tubules open into the vasa efferentia through the rete testis. Vasa efferentia leave the testis and open into the epididymis on the posterior surface of each testis. The epididymis leads to the vas deferens, which ascends to the abdomen and loops over the urinary bladder.

The vas deferens receives a duct from the seminal vesicle and opens into the urethra as the ejaculatory duct. These ducts store and transport sperms from the testis to the outside through the urethra, which runs from the urinary bladder through the penis to its external opening, the urethral meatus.

The penis is the male external genitalia, made of special tissue that helps in erection to facilitate insemination. Its enlarged end, the glans penis, is covered by a loose fold of skin called the foreskin.

Male accessory glands: paired seminal vesicles, a prostate and paired bulbourethral glands. Their secretions form the seminal plasma, rich in fructose, calcium and certain enzymes. Bulbourethral secretions also help lubricate the penis.

example.answer: Seminiferous tubule → rete testis → vasa efferentia → epididymis → vas deferens → ejaculatory duct → urethra → urethral meatus

learn.hook: The fallopian tube's fimbriae act like a catcher's glove at a cricket match, sweeping in the ovum released from the ovary.
points: The female reproductive system has a pair of ovaries, accessory ducts (oviducts, uterus, vagina), external genitalia and mammary glands, all located in the pelvic region (mammary glands excepted).

Ovaries are the primary female sex organs: they produce the female gamete (ovum) and several steroid hormones (ovarian hormones). Each ovary is about 2–4 cm long, connected to the pelvic wall and uterus by ligaments. A thin epithelium encloses the ovarian stroma, which has a peripheral cortex and an inner medulla.

Each fallopian tube (oviduct) is about 10–12 cm long. Near the ovary is the funnel-shaped infundibulum with finger-like fimbriae that help collect the ovum after ovulation. It leads to the wider ampulla, and the last narrow part, the isthmus, joins the uterus.
The uterus (womb) is single and shaped like an inverted pear. It opens into the vagina through a narrow cervix; the cervical canal together with the vagina forms the birth canal.

The uterine wall has three layers: outer thin perimetrium; middle thick smooth-muscle myometrium, which contracts strongly during delivery; and inner glandular endometrium, which lines the cavity and undergoes cyclic changes during the menstrual cycle.

The thin membranous outer layer is the perimetrium.
example.answer: (a) Endometrium (b) Myometrium (c) Perimetrium

points: Female external genitalia: mons pubis (a cushion of fatty tissue covered by skin and pubic hair), labia majora (fleshy folds extending down from the mons pubis and surrounding the vaginal opening), labia minora (paired folds under the labia majora), hymen (a membrane that often partially covers the vaginal opening) and clitoris (a tiny finger-like structure at the upper junction of the labia minora, above the urethral opening).

The hymen can tear due to many reasons, such as a sudden fall or jolt, insertion of a tampon or active sports like cycling or horse riding; in some women it persists even after coitus. So the presence or absence of a hymen is not a reliable indicator of virginity or sexual experience.

Mammary glands are paired structures containing glandular tissue and variable amounts of fat. The glandular tissue of each breast is divided into 15–20 mammary lobes containing clusters of cells called alveoli, which secrete milk stored in their lumens.
Milk pathway: alveoli → mammary tubules → mammary duct (tubules of each lobe join) → mammary ampulla (several ducts join) → lactiferous duct, through which milk is sucked out.

learn.hook: A healthy adult male makes millions of sperms every day, and the switch for this factory sits in the brain.
points: Spermatogenesis begins at puberty in the testes. Spermatogonia (2n = 46) on the inner wall of seminiferous tubules multiply by mitosis.

Some spermatogonia, now called primary spermatocytes (2n), undergo meiosis. The first meiotic (reduction) division gives two equal haploid secondary spermatocytes, each with 23 chromosomes. The second meiotic division gives four equal haploid spermatids.
Spermiogenesis: spermatids are transformed into spermatozoa (sperms). Sperm heads become embedded in Sertoli cells, and sperms are finally released from the seminiferous tubules by spermiation.

Hormonal control: at puberty the hypothalamus increases secretion of GnRH (gonadotropin releasing hormone). GnRH acts on the anterior pituitary to release LH and FSH. LH acts on Leydig cells to stimulate androgen synthesis; androgens stimulate spermatogenesis. FSH acts on Sertoli cells and stimulates secretion of factors that help spermiogenesis.

example.answer: 200 sperms, each with 23 chromosomes.

topics.title: Structure of a sperm and labelled diagrams

learn.hook: A sperm is a tiny self-driving vehicle: a payload in the head, a battery pack in the middle piece and a propeller for a tail.
points: A sperm has a head, neck, middle piece and tail, all enveloped by a plasma membrane. The head contains an elongated haploid nucleus, and its anterior portion is covered by a cap-like acrosome filled with enzymes that help fertilisation.
The middle piece has numerous mitochondria, which produce energy for tail movement, giving sperm motility essential for fertilisation.

A human male ejaculates about 200 to 300 million sperms during coitus. For normal fertility at least 60 per cent of them must have normal shape and size and at least 40 per cent must show vigorous motility.

Secretions of the epididymis, vas deferens, seminal vesicle and prostate are essential for maturation and motility of sperms. Seminal plasma + sperms = semen. Androgens maintain the functions of male accessory ducts and glands.

Diagram practice for boards: male and female reproductive systems, sperm (acrosome, nucleus, neck, middle piece with mitochondria, tail), Graafian follicle (antrum, secondary oocyte, zona pellucida, theca), blastocyst (trophoblast, inner cell mass, blastocoel).

example.answer: At least 150 million normal; at least 100 million vigorously motile.

learn.hook: A baby girl is born with all her primary oocytes already made. No new oogonia are ever added after birth.
points: Oogenesis starts during embryonic development: a couple of million oogonia form in each foetal ovary, and no more are added after birth. Oogonia start meiosis, enter prophase I and are temporarily arrested as primary oocytes.

Each primary oocyte gets surrounded by a layer of granulosa cells to form a primary follicle. Many follicles degenerate from birth to puberty, so only 60,000–80,000 primary follicles remain in each ovary at puberty.

Primary follicles get more layers of granulosa cells and a new theca to become secondary follicles. A secondary follicle becomes a tertiary follicle with a fluid-filled cavity, the antrum; its theca organises into an inner theca interna and outer theca externa.

Within the tertiary follicle, the primary oocyte completes meiosis I, an unequal division forming a large haploid secondary oocyte and a tiny first polar body. The tertiary follicle matures into a Graafian follicle; the secondary oocyte forms a new membrane, the zona pellucida. The Graafian follicle ruptures to release the secondary oocyte (ovum) by ovulation.

Comparison: spermatogenesis begins at puberty and continues lifelong; one primary spermatocyte gives four sperms by equal divisions. Oogenesis begins before birth, is arrested and resumes cyclically; one primary oocyte gives only one ovum with polar bodies, because of unequal divisions.

example.q: How many functional female gametes and how many male gametes are formed from 10 primary oocytes and 10 primary spermatocytes respectively?
steps: Each primary oocyte yields 1 functional ovum (other products are polar bodies): 10 × 1 = 10.
Each primary spermatocyte yields 4 sperms: 10 × 4 = 40.
example.answer: 10 ova and 40 sperms.

topics.title: The menstrual cycle: menstrual and follicular phases

learn.hook: Many teens track their cycles on phone apps. Behind every app's calendar is a hormone story this topic explains.
points: The menstrual cycle is the reproductive cycle of female primates (monkeys, apes and humans). The first menstruation at puberty is menarche. A cycle repeats on average every 28/29 days; one ovum is usually released in the middle of each cycle.
Menstrual phase: lasts 3–5 days; the endometrial lining of the uterus and its blood vessels break down and leave as menstrual flow. It occurs only if the released ovum is not fertilised.
Lack of menstruation may indicate pregnancy, but it may also be caused by other underlying causes like stress or poor health.

Follicular (proliferative) phase: after menstruation, primary follicles grow into a fully mature Graafian follicle and the endometrium regenerates by proliferation. Pituitary gonadotropins (LH and FSH) increase gradually, stimulating follicle development and secretion of oestrogens by growing follicles.
Cycles stop around 50 years of age (menopause). Cyclic menstruation between menarche and menopause is an indicator of the normal reproductive phase.

example.q: A student's cycle is 28 days and the menstrual flow lasts 4 days. Using the standard model, on roughly which day does ovulation occur and which phase covers days 5–13?
steps: In a 28-day cycle, the LH surge and ovulation occur around day 14.
Days 1–4 = menstrual phase.
Days 5–13 = follicular (proliferative) phase, with follicle growth and endometrial regeneration.
example.answer: Ovulation about day 14; days 5–13 are the follicular phase.

topics.title: Ovulation, the luteal phase and hormone graphs

learn.hook: Mid-cycle, one hormone spikes so sharply that doctors call it a 'surge'. That spike is the trigger for ovulation.
points: Both LH and FSH reach a peak in the middle of the cycle (about day 14). The rapid rise of LH to its maximum, the LH surge, induces rupture of the Graafian follicle and release of the ovum (ovulation). This is the ovulatory phase.

Luteal (secretory) phase: the remaining parts of the ruptured Graafian follicle transform into the corpus luteum, which secretes large amounts of progesterone. Progesterone maintains the endometrium, which is needed for implantation and other events of pregnancy.
During pregnancy, all events of the menstrual cycle stop and there is no menstruation.
In the absence of fertilisation, the corpus luteum degenerates. Progesterone falls, the endometrium disintegrates, and menstruation begins a new cycle.
Graph reading: oestrogen rises in the follicular phase; LH (and FSH) peak sharply near day 14; progesterone is highest in the luteal phase and falls before menstruation.

example.q: On a hormone graph of a 28-day cycle, curve X peaks sharply at day 14; curve Y stays low until day 15, rises to a peak around day 21 and falls by day 28. Identify X and Y and their sources.
steps: A sharp mid-cycle peak that triggers ovulation is the LH surge, from the anterior pituitary.
A hormone high only after ovulation is from the corpus luteum: progesterone.
example.answer: X = LH (anterior pituitary); Y = progesterone (corpus luteum)

learn.hook: The sex of a baby is decided at the instant of fertilisation, and it is the sperm, not the ovum, that decides it.
points: Insemination: during coitus, semen is released by the penis into the vagina. Motile sperms swim through the cervix and uterus to the ampullary region of the fallopian tube. The ovum released by the ovary is also transported to the ampulla, where fertilisation takes place.
Fertilisation can occur only if the ovum and sperms reach the ampullary region at the same time. This is why not all copulations lead to fertilisation and pregnancy.

When a sperm contacts the zona pellucida, changes in the membrane block entry of additional sperms (preventing polyspermy). Acrosome secretions help the sperm enter the cytoplasm of the ovum through the zona pellucida and plasma membrane.

Sperm entry induces the secondary oocyte to complete meiosis II. This second division is also unequal, giving a second polar body and a haploid ovum (ootid). The haploid nuclei of sperm and ovum fuse to form a diploid zygote.

Sex: females are XX, males XY. All ova carry X. Half the sperms carry X and half carry Y. X sperm + ovum → XX (female); Y sperm + ovum → XY (male). So the sex of the baby is decided by the father's sperm.

example.q: What is the probability that a couple's next child will be a girl, and which parent's gamete decides it?
steps: All ova carry X.
50% of sperms carry X, 50% carry Y.
Girl (XX) needs an X sperm: probability 1/2.
example.answer: 1/2 (50%); decided by the father's sperm.

learn.reallife: Families sometimes wrongly blame mothers for not having a son; biology shows the father's sperm decides the sex, a point stressed in health-awareness campaigns across India.

learn.hook: In just a few days, one zygote becomes a ball of cells that burrows into the uterine wall like a seed planting itself.
points: Cleavage: mitotic divisions start as the zygote moves through the isthmus of the oviduct towards the uterus, forming 2, 4, 8, 16 daughter cells called blastomeres. The embryo with 8 to 16 blastomeres is the morula.

The morula keeps dividing and becomes a blastocyst as it moves further into the uterus. Blastomeres in the blastocyst are arranged as an outer layer, the trophoblast, and an inner group of cells attached to it, the inner cell mass.

The trophoblast attaches to the endometrium, and the inner cell mass differentiates into the embryo. After attachment, uterine cells divide rapidly and cover the blastocyst. The blastocyst becomes embedded in the endometrium: implantation. This leads to pregnancy.
Board trace: fertilisation (ampulla) → cleavage (while moving through the isthmus) → morula → blastocyst (in uterus) → implantation (in endometrium).

example.q: After how many rounds of cleavage will the embryo first reach the 16-cell stage, assuming all blastomeres divide together?
steps: Each round doubles the cells: 1 → 2 → 4 → 8 → 16.
That is four rounds.
example.answer: 4 rounds of cleavage (2⁴ = 16).

learn.hook: The placenta is an organ that exists only during pregnancy, yet it does the jobs of lungs, gut, kidneys and an endocrine gland for the foetus.
points: After implantation, finger-like projections called chorionic villi appear on the trophoblast, surrounded by uterine tissue and maternal blood. The chorionic villi and uterine tissue interdigitate and jointly form the placenta, a structural and functional unit between the developing embryo (foetus) and the mother's body.
The placenta is connected to the embryo through the umbilical cord, which transports substances to and from the embryo.
Placental functions: supplies oxygen and nutrients to the embryo; removes carbon dioxide and excretory or waste materials produced by the embryo; acts as an endocrine tissue.

Placental hormones: human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG), human placental lactogen (hPL), oestrogens and progestogens. In the later phase of pregnancy, the ovary secretes relaxin. hCG, hPL and relaxin are produced in women only during pregnancy.

Pregnancy also raises maternal levels of other hormones like oestrogens, progestogens, cortisol, prolactin and thyroxine. These are needed for foetal growth, maternal metabolic changes and maintenance of pregnancy.

example.answer: hCG; from the placenta; produced only during pregnancy.

learn.hook: By the end of the first trimester, a foetus smaller than your palm already has most of its major organ systems.
points: Immediately after implantation, the inner cell mass differentiates into an outer ectoderm and an inner endoderm; a mesoderm soon appears between them. These three germ layers give rise to all tissues (organs) in adults.
The inner cell mass contains stem cells, which have the potency to give rise to all tissues and organs.

Milestones of human pregnancy (about 9 months): after one month, the heart forms; the first sign of a growing foetus may be noticed by listening to the heart sound with a stethoscope. By the end of the second month, limbs and digits develop.

By the end of 12 weeks (first trimester), most major organ systems form, e.g. limbs and external genital organs are well developed. The first foetal movements and hair on the head usually appear in the fifth month.
By the end of 24 weeks (second trimester), the body is covered with fine hair, eyelids separate and eyelashes form. By the end of nine months the foetus is fully developed and ready for delivery.

learn.hook: Childbirth is one of the few processes in the body that run on positive feedback: each contraction calls for a stronger one.
points: Parturition is the delivery of the foetus by vigorous contractions of the uterus at the end of pregnancy. It is induced by a complex neuroendocrine mechanism.
Signals for parturition originate from the fully developed foetus and the placenta, inducing mild uterine contractions called the foetal ejection reflex.

This reflex triggers release of oxytocin from the maternal pituitary. Oxytocin acts on uterine muscle, causing stronger contractions, which in turn stimulate further oxytocin secretion. This continues until the baby is expelled through the birth canal; soon after, the placenta is also expelled.

Mammary glands differentiate during pregnancy and start producing milk towards its end (lactation). Milk produced in the first few days is colostrum, which contains several antibodies (notably IgA) absolutely essential to develop resistance in newborn babies. Breastfeeding during early growth is recommended by doctors for a healthy baby.

example.q: Explain why oxytocin release during labour is called a positive feedback loop.
steps: The foetal ejection reflex triggers oxytocin release.
Oxytocin makes the uterus contract more strongly.
Stronger contractions stimulate even more oxytocin release, amplifying the response until delivery.
example.answer: The output (stronger contraction) increases the stimulus (oxytocin), so the response keeps intensifying until delivery.

learn.reallife: Hospitals across India counsel mothers to breastfeed within the first hour, so the newborn gets antibody-rich colostrum.

learn.hook: India started a national family planning programme in 1951, one of the first countries in the world to do so.
points: According to the World Health Organisation (WHO), reproductive health means total well-being in all aspects of reproduction: physical, emotional, behavioural and social. A society with people having physically and functionally normal reproductive organs and normal emotional and behavioural interactions in all sex-related aspects is reproductively healthy.

India initiated action plans and programmes at a national level to attain total reproductive health in 1951 under the name 'family planning'. Improved programmes covering wider areas are now run as Reproductive and Child Health Care (RCH) programmes.

Strategies: create awareness through audio-visual and print media with government and non-government agencies; parents, close relatives, teachers and friends also have a big role in sharing information.

Introduce sex education in schools to give correct information about reproductive organs, adolescence and related changes, safe and hygienic sexual practices, STDs and AIDS, so young people are not misled by myths and misconceptions.

Educate fertile couples and those of marriageable age about birth control options, care of pregnant mothers, post-natal care of mother and child, importance of breastfeeding and equal opportunities for male and female children; spread awareness about problems of uncontrolled population growth and social evils like sex abuse and sex-related crimes.

example.q: A school plans a reproductive-health week. Suggest three activities that match the strategies in NCERT.
steps: Awareness: poster and video sessions with help from health agencies.
Sex education: a doctor explains adolescence, reproductive organs, safe and hygienic practices and STIs, busting myths.
Social messages: talks on equal opportunity for girls and boys and on the problems of uncontrolled population growth.
example.answer: Awareness sessions, factual sex education by experts, and talks on gender equality and population issues.

learn.reallife: School health programmes such as Ayushman Bharat's School Health and Wellness initiative give adolescents accurate, age-appropriate information, replacing playground myths.

topics.title: Amniocentesis ban and gains in reproductive health

learn.hook: A test meant to detect genetic disorders was misused to identify the sex of a foetus, so India banned that particular use by law.
points: Amniocentesis is a foetal test based on the chromosomal pattern in the amniotic fluid surrounding the developing embryo. It can detect genetic disorders.
There is a statutory (legal) ban on amniocentesis for sex determination, to check the rise in female foeticide. Massive child immunisation is another major step.

Research on reproduction-related areas is encouraged by government and non-government agencies to find newer methods. For example, Saheli, a new oral contraceptive for females, was developed by scientists at the Central Drug Research Institute (CDRI), Lucknow.

Results: better awareness about sex-related matters; more medically assisted deliveries and better post-natal care, lowering maternal and infant mortality rates; more couples with small families; better detection and cure of STDs; increased medical facilities for sex-related problems.

example.q: Why is amniocentesis allowed for detecting genetic disorders but banned for sex determination?
steps: Detecting chromosomal or genetic disorders helps doctors and parents manage health risks.
Using it to find the foetus's sex was leading to selective abortion of female foetuses.
The statutory ban targets the misuse, protecting the sex ratio and the rights of girls.
example.answer: Medical use protects health; the ban stops misuse for sex determination and female foeticide.

learn.reallife: Signboards in Indian clinics read 'Sex determination is a punishable offence' because of this ban.

learn.hook: According to NCERT, India's population was about 350 million at Independence and crossed 1.2 billion in May 2011.
points: Better living conditions led to a population explosion. Causes: a rapid decline in death rate, maternal mortality rate (MMR) and infant mortality rate (IMR), and an increase in the number of people in the reproductive age.

NCERT figures: world population about 2 billion in 1900, about 6 billion by 2000 and 7.2 billion in 2011. India: about 350 million at Independence, close to the billion mark by 2000, and over 1.2 billion by May 2011.
The 2011 census shows India's population growth rate was less than 2 per cent, i.e. 20/1000/year. Uncontrolled growth leads to scarcity of basic requirements like food, shelter and clothing.

Measures: motivating smaller families with contraceptive methods; slogans like 'Hum Do Hamare Do' and many urban couples adopting a 'one child norm'; statutory raising of the marriageable age of females to 18 years and of males to 21 years; incentives given to couples with small families.

example.q: A growth rate of 20 per 1000 per year is the same as what percentage? If a town has 50,000 people, how many are added in a year at this rate?
example.answer: 2 per cent; about 1000 people per year.

topics.title: The ideal contraceptive and natural methods

learn.hook: Not every method of family planning needs a pharmacy; some depend only on understanding the body's own cycle.
points: An ideal contraceptive should be user-friendly, easily available, effective and reversible, with no or least side effects, and it should in no way interfere with sexual drive, desire or the sexual act of the user.
Contraceptive methods are classified as natural/traditional, barrier, IUDs, oral contraceptives, injectables, implants and surgical methods.

Natural methods avoid meeting of ovum and sperms. Periodic abstinence: avoiding coitus from day 10 to 17 of the menstrual cycle, when ovulation is expected (the fertile period). Withdrawal or coitus interruptus: the male withdraws his penis before ejaculation.

Lactational amenorrhea: absence of menstruation during intense lactation following parturition. Since ovulation and the cycle do not occur, chances of conception are almost nil. It is theoretically effective only up to a maximum of six months after parturition, as long as the mother breastfeeds the child fully.
Natural methods have almost no side effects, but their chances of failure are high.

example.q: A woman has a regular 28-day cycle. Using periodic abstinence as described in NCERT, which days should be avoided and why?
steps: Ovulation is expected around day 14.

example.answer: Days 10 to 17, because chances of fertilisation are very high around ovulation.

learn.hook: A small copper-bearing device placed in the uterus is among the most widely accepted contraceptive methods in India.
points: Barrier methods physically prevent ovum and sperms from meeting. Condoms are barriers of thin rubber or latex used to cover the penis in males or the vagina and cervix in females just before coitus, so semen is not released into the female tract. 'Nirodh' is a popular brand for males.
Condoms also safeguard the user from contracting STIs and AIDS. Both male and female condoms are disposable and can be self-inserted, giving privacy to the user.

Diaphragms, cervical caps and vaults are rubber barriers inserted into the female reproductive tract to cover the cervix during coitus, blocking sperm entry. They are reusable. Spermicidal creams, jellies and foams are usually used with them to increase efficiency.

Intrauterine devices (IUDs) are inserted by doctors or expert nurses into the uterus through the vagina. Types: non-medicated (Lippes loop), copper-releasing (CuT, Cu7, Multiload 375) and hormone-releasing (Progestasert, LNG-20).

IUDs increase phagocytosis of sperms within the uterus. Released Cu ions suppress sperm motility and fertilising capacity. Hormone-releasing IUDs make the uterus unsuitable for implantation and the cervix hostile to sperms. IUDs suit females who want to delay pregnancy and/or space children.

topics.title: Pills, injectables, emergency and surgical methods

learn.hook: A once-a-week contraceptive pill developed in Lucknow is called Saheli, meaning 'friend'.
points: Oral contraceptives contain progestogens or progestogen–oestrogen combinations. They are taken daily for 21 days, starting preferably within the first five days of the menstrual cycle; after a gap of 7 days (during which menstruation occurs) the course is repeated. They inhibit ovulation and implantation and alter the quality of cervical mucus to prevent or retard entry of sperms.

Saheli, the new oral contraceptive for females, contains a non-steroidal preparation and is a 'once a week' pill with very few side effects and high contraceptive value. It was developed at CDRI, Lucknow.

Progestogens alone or with oestrogen can also be used as injections or implants under the skin, acting like pills over a longer period. Progestogens or progestogen–oestrogen combinations or IUDs used within 72 hours of coitus are very effective emergency contraceptives, used after rape or casual unprotected intercourse.

Surgical (terminal) methods, or sterilisation, are for those who want no more children. Vasectomy: a small part of the vas deferens is removed or tied up through a small incision on the scrotum. Tubectomy: a small part of the fallopian tube is removed or tied up through a small incision in the abdomen or through the vagina. They are highly effective, but reversibility is very poor.

Possible side effects of contraceptives include nausea, abdominal pain, breakthrough bleeding, irregular menstrual bleeding and even breast cancer. So contraceptives should be used only after proper medical advice.

example.q: Name the method: (a) part of the vas deferens tied through a scrotal incision; (b) pill taken weekly; (c) used within 72 hours after unprotected coitus.
steps: (a) Cutting or tying the vas deferens is vasectomy.
(b) The non-steroidal weekly pill is Saheli.
(c) Hormones or an IUD used within 72 hours act as emergency contraceptives.
example.answer: (a) Vasectomy (b) Saheli (c) Emergency contraception

learn.reallife: India's family planning programme offers both vasectomy and tubectomy free at government hospitals; no-scalpel vasectomy is promoted because it is quick and minimally invasive.

learn.hook: Laws on MTP aim at one goal: reducing unsafe abortions that endanger women's lives.
points: Intentional or voluntary termination of pregnancy before full term is called medical termination of pregnancy (MTP) or induced abortion. Nearly 45 to 50 million MTPs are performed in a year worldwide, about one-fifth of all conceived pregnancies.

India legalised MTP in 1971 with strict conditions. NCERT describes the MTP (Amendment) Act, 2017: a pregnancy may be terminated within the first 12 weeks on the opinion of one registered medical practitioner; between 12 and 24 weeks, two registered medical practitioners must agree that the grounds exist. (The law was updated again in 2021; for board answers, use the NCERT version.)

Grounds: continuing the pregnancy would risk the woman's life or cause grave injury to her physical or mental health; or there is substantial risk that the child would suffer from serious physical or mental abnormalities.

MTP helps get rid of unwanted pregnancies due to casual unprotected intercourse or failure of contraception, and in cases where continuation could be harmful or fatal to the mother, the foetus or both. MTPs are considered relatively safe during the first trimester (up to 12 weeks).

Concerns: misuse to abort normal female foetuses; many MTPs performed illegally by unqualified quacks, which are unsafe and could be fatal; emotional, ethical, religious and social issues. Using MTP as a contraceptive substitute is dangerous; counselling and safe facilities are important.

example.q: According to NCERT's description of the MTP (Amendment) Act, 2017, how many registered medical practitioners must give an opinion for terminating a pregnancy of (a) 10 weeks and (b) 18 weeks?
steps: (a) 10 weeks is within the first 12 weeks: one registered medical practitioner.
(b) 18 weeks lies between 12 and 24 weeks: two registered medical practitioners.
example.answer: (a) One (b) Two

learn.reallife: The law aims to move abortions from unsafe quacks to qualified doctors in registered facilities, protecting women's lives.

learn.hook: NCERT notes that STIs are most common in the 15 to 24 age group, which is why correct information matters early.
points: Infections transmitted through sexual intercourse are called sexually transmitted infections (STIs), venereal diseases (VD) or reproductive tract infections (RTI). Examples: gonorrhoea, syphilis, genital herpes, chlamydiasis, genital warts, trichomoniasis, hepatitis-B and HIV leading to AIDS.
Some, like hepatitis-B and HIV, also spread by sharing injection needles or surgical instruments with infected persons, transfusion of blood, or from an infected mother to the foetus.
Except for hepatitis-B, genital herpes and HIV infections, the other diseases are completely curable if detected early and treated properly.

Early symptoms are often minor: itching, fluid discharge, slight pain and swellings in the genital region. Infected females may be asymptomatic, so the disease stays undetected. Social stigma also stops people from seeking timely treatment. Untreated STIs can lead to pelvic inflammatory diseases (PID), abortions, still births, ectopic pregnancies, infertility or even cancer of the reproductive tract.
Prevention: avoid sex with unknown partners or multiple partners; always try to use condoms during coitus; in case of doubt, go to a qualified doctor for early detection and complete treatment.

example.q: Which of these STIs are NOT completely curable even when detected early: gonorrhoea, genital herpes, syphilis, hepatitis-B, HIV, chlamydiasis?
steps: NCERT exceptions: hepatitis-B, genital herpes and HIV.

example.answer: Genital herpes, hepatitis-B and HIV

learn.reallife: NACO and state health departments run free, confidential STI clinics (Suraksha clinics) so young people can get tested without fear of stigma.

learn.hook: The world's first IVF baby was born in 1978; today Indian IVF clinics help thousands of couples every year.
points: Infertility: many couples cannot produce children in spite of unprotected sexual co-habitation. Causes may be physical, congenital, diseases, drugs, immunological or even psychological. In India the female is often blamed, but the cause can lie with either partner; NCERT stresses that very often the problem lies with the male partner.
Specialised health care units (infertility clinics) can diagnose and correct some disorders; where no correction is possible, assisted reproductive technologies (ART) can help.

In vitro fertilisation (IVF) is fertilisation outside the body in conditions similar to those in the body, followed by embryo transfer (ET). It is popularly called the 'test tube baby' programme. Ova from the wife or a donor and sperms from the husband or a donor are collected and induced to form a zygote in the laboratory.

ZIFT (zygote intra fallopian transfer): the zygote or early embryo with up to 8 blastomeres is transferred into the fallopian tube. IUT (intra uterine transfer): embryos with more than 8 blastomeres are transferred into the uterus.

example.q: An IVF lab has two embryos: one at 6 blastomeres and one at 32 blastomeres. Which transfer technique suits each?
steps: Up to 8 blastomeres → ZIFT, into the fallopian tube.
More than 8 blastomeres → IUT, into the uterus.
example.answer: 6-cell embryo: ZIFT; 32-cell embryo: IUT.

learn.reallife: Indian regulation of ART clinics, under the ART (Regulation) Act, 2021, sets standards so couples receive safe, ethical treatment.

learn.hook: Science can now inject a single sperm into an ovum with a needle thinner than a hair. That is ICSI.
points: Embryos formed by in vivo fertilisation (fusion of gametes within the female) can also be used for such transfers to help females who cannot conceive.

GIFT (gamete intra fallopian transfer): an ovum collected from a donor is transferred into the fallopian tube of another female who cannot produce ova but can provide a suitable environment for fertilisation and further development.
ICSI (intra cytoplasmic sperm injection): a specialised procedure in which a sperm is directly injected into the ovum to form an embryo in the laboratory.

Artificial insemination (AI): used when the male partner cannot inseminate the female or has a very low sperm count. Semen from the husband or a healthy donor is artificially introduced into the vagina or into the uterus; the latter is IUI (intra-uterine insemination).

Limitations of ART: needs extremely high precision handling by specialised professionals and expensive instruments, so facilities exist only in few centres and are affordable to limited people; emotional, religious and social factors also deter. Legal adoption is one of the best options for couples seeking parenthood, as many orphaned and destitute children need care.

example.q: Match each problem to an ART: (a) very low sperm count; (b) a woman cannot produce ova but her tubes and uterus are healthy; (c) sperms cannot penetrate the ovum on their own.
steps: (a) Low sperm count: artificial insemination, e.g. IUI.
(b) No ova but suitable environment: GIFT with a donor ovum.
(c) Sperms unable to fertilise: ICSI, injecting a sperm into the ovum.
example.answer: (a) AI/IUI (b) GIFT (c) ICSI

learn.reallife: India's Juvenile Justice Act and the CARA portal let couples legally adopt children, which NCERT highlights as a valuable alternative to ART.
